clinicalPearls: Extraspinal compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve within the deep gluteal space, classically as it relates to the piriformis muscle, producing buttock pain with radiation down the posterior leg.
Deep, aching buttock pain aggravated by prolonged sitting, and tenderness over the sciatic notch, are more characteristic than the dermatomal back pain of lumbar radiculopathy.

The Freiberg sign (pain on passive internal rotation of the extended hip) and the Pace sign (pain and weakness on resisted abduction and external rotation of the flexed hip) are supportive provocative tests.
The FAIR position (flexion, adduction and internal rotation) reproduces symptoms and is sometimes combined with electrophysiological H-reflex testing.
An anatomical variant in which the peroneal division pierces the piriformis is common and may predispose to entrapment.
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion made only after lumbosacral radiculopathy and other causes of sciatica have been carefully ruled out.
Magnetic resonance neurography and open or ultrasound-guided injections can support the diagnosis but none is fully specific.
Symptoms typically lack the true neurological deficit of a compressive disc lesion, with preserved reflexes and only subjective sensory change in many cases.
reference.pathophysiology: The sciatic nerve exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen in intimate relation to the piriformis muscle within the deep gluteal (subgluteal) space. Hypertrophy, spasm, fibrosis, anatomical variation of the nerve or muscle, trauma, or a space-occupying lesion can compress or tether the nerve, producing mechanical irritation and secondary ischaemia. Fibrous bands and other deep gluteal structures may contribute, and the broader concept of deep gluteal syndrome recognises multiple potential sites of extraspinal sciatic entrapment. The result is buttock pain with variable referred symptoms along the sciatic distribution, usually without the discrete root-level deficit of intraspinal pathology.
additionalDifferentials: lumbosacral radiculopathy from disc herniation or stenosis
gluteal or pelvic neoplasm compressing the sciatic nerve
additionalInvestigations: lumbosacral spine magnetic resonance imaging to exclude radiculopathy
magnetic resonance neurography of the lumbosacral plexus and sciatic nerve
electromyography and nerve conduction studies including H-reflex, with FAIR-position testing
pelvic and hip imaging to exclude articular or mass lesions
diagnostic ultrasound-guided perisciatic or intramuscular injection
dynamic ultrasound of the deep gluteal space
inflammatory and metabolic screen when a systemic cause is considered
redFlags: progressive foot drop or objective motor weakness suggesting significant nerve compromise
bowel or bladder disturbance or saddle anaesthesia indicating cauda equina pathology
night pain, weight loss or a palpable mass suggesting pelvic or gluteal malignancy
bilateral symptoms or systemic features pointing to an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve with physiotherapy, activity modification and targeted injections, and prognosis is generally favourable. A minority with refractory symptoms may require surgical decompression, with variable outcomes.
pitfalls: diagnosing piriformis syndrome before adequately excluding lumbosacral radiculopathy
over-reliance on provocative signs that are neither sensitive nor specific
attributing all deep gluteal sciatic symptoms to the piriformis when other structures may be responsible
missing a pelvic or gluteal tumour presenting as apparent entrapment
references: Dawson, Hallett and Wilbourn: Entrapment Neuropathies
